Anyway, when I got back to my desk, my laptop had gone to sleep and the report had not saved. I lost about forty minutes of work. So now I press save every five minutes, and I do not make toast at work.

b1-w3-bc0.speaker: Manager
b1-w3-bc0.text: Before you go, here is next week, so nobody is surprised. On Monday the auditors are coming at nine. That is arranged, it is in the calendar, and they are staying until Wednesday. While they are here, please do not move any files out of the shared folder. On Tuesday I am meeting the two new suppliers, so I will not be at my desk in the morning. If you need me, send a message and I will answer between meetings. Wednesday is the big one: we are presenting the quarter figures at two o'clock, and I am going to ask Yusuf to open, because he built the numbers. Thursday will probably be quiet, so that is a good day to finish anything the auditors ask for. And on Friday the office is closing at one, because the lift is being repaired in the afternoon. One last thing. I am not going to send a reminder about the timesheets again. They are due Thursday. Please just do them.

b1-w4-bc0.speaker: Examiner
b1-w4-bc0.text: Right, listen carefully, because these rules decide whether you sit the exam or not. If you arrive more than thirty minutes late, you will not be allowed into the hall. If you arrive before that, you can come in, but you will not get extra time. As soon as you sit down, put your identity card on the desk, face up. If an invigilator cannot see your card, they will stop and ask you, and that wastes your time, not theirs. Phones: if your phone makes any sound, even inside your bag, the exam is over for you. There is no warning and there is no second chance. When you finish, stay in your seat until an invigilator collects your paper. If you stand up and walk to the front, your paper may be counted as incomplete. Finally, if you feel unwell during the exam, raise your hand and wait. Do not leave the hall on your own, because once you go through that door you cannot come back in.

b1-w5-bc0.speaker: Host
b1-w5-bc0.text: Good afternoon. Today's question is simple. If you found a bag with a lot of money in it, what would you do? The lines are open. First caller, you are on.

b1-w5-bc1.speaker: Hisham
b1-w5-bc1.text: Hello. I would take it straight to the police. I know some people would keep it, but I would not sleep. If it were my bag, I would want somebody to do the same for me. My father lost his wallet in a taxi twenty years ago, and a stranger returned it with everything inside. If that had not happened, I think I would be a different person today.

b1-w5-bc2.speaker: Dina
b1-w5-bc2.text: I would take it to the police too, but I want to be honest: I would think about it first. If I had no money for the rent that month, it would be much harder. I do not think people who keep it are all bad. I think they are frightened. If we talked about money more openly, fewer people would be in that situation.

b1-w5-bc3.speaker: Host
b1-w5-bc3.text: Two answers, and neither of them is as simple as it sounds. More after the news.

b1-w6-bc0.speaker: Reporter
b1-w6-bc0.text: Every city has a house like this one. It stands at the end of a quiet street, the windows are covered, and the garden has not been cut for at least ten years. Nobody in the neighbourhood can tell us who owns it. It must belong to somebody: the taxes are paid every year, on time, from a bank in another city. So the owner might be living abroad, or the house could be part of an old family argument that no lawyer has been able to finish. What is certain is that it cannot be abandoned, because abandoned houses do not pay their taxes. Neighbours say a car comes twice a year, always in the evening. A woman gets out, stays for about an hour, and leaves. She might be the owner. She may be a lawyer. She could simply be someone who was asked, a long time ago, to check that the roof is still there. We knocked on the door for three days. Nobody answered, and yet somebody, somewhere, is still paying.

b1-w7-bc0.speaker: Host
b1-w7-bc0.text: You have been repairing bicycles in the same shop for nine years. How did it start?

b1-w7-bc1.speaker: Guest
b1-w7-bc1.text: By accident. I had been working in an office for six years, and I hated it. I had been fixing my own bike since I was a boy, and one evening a neighbour asked me to look at hers. Then her brother came. Then his friends. I have been doing it ever since. For the first two years I was still in the office, so I was repairing bikes until midnight and going to work tired. I have been teaching a class on Saturdays for about eighteen months now, and that is the part I enjoy most. People arrive thinking a bicycle is complicated. It is not. It has been more or less the same machine for a hundred years, and it wants to be understood, not respected.

b1-w7-bc2.speaker: Host
b1-w7-bc2.text: And the office? Do you ever miss it?

b1-w7-bc3.speaker: Guest
b1-w7-bc3.text: I have not thought about the office for years. That is the answer.

b1-w8-bc0.speaker: Presenter
b1-w8-bc0.text: In nineteen eighty-five, this street had four bakeries. Today it has one, and it opens at six because the man who runs it still cannot sleep past five. People here will tell you that things used to be better, and then, if you sit with them long enough, they will tell you something more honest. Mrs Aziza used to sell vegetables from a table outside her door. She would start at four in the morning, and in winter her hands would crack. She does not miss that. What she misses is the noise: the children who used to play in the road because there were almost no cars, and the neighbours who would sit outside until midnight in summer because nobody had air conditioning. Her grandson has a good job and a flat with cold air and a lock on the door, and she is proud of him. But he does not know the names of the people upstairs. She used to know everybody in three streets. That is the thing nobody planned to lose.

b1-w9-bc0.speaker: Presenter
b1-w9-bc0.text: This week we compared two lives: a teacher in Cairo and her sister, who teaches in a village three hours away. The results were not as simple as we expected. The village teacher earns almost thirty per cent less, but she saves more than her sister, because her rent is nowhere near as high. The city teacher's flat costs more than half her salary. On the other hand, the village school has far fewer resources: no library, one computer, and classes that are not nearly as small as people imagine, at forty-two children in one room. The city classes are bigger still, at forty-eight. Both sisters said the same thing about time. The city teacher spends two hours a day travelling; the village teacher walks for eleven minutes. That is the biggest difference of all, and it is the one nobody puts in a salary. So which life is better? Neither. The village is cheaper and slower, the city is richer and harder, and the honest answer is that they are not really the same job.

b1-w10-bc0.speaker: Guide
b1-w10-bc0.text: Stop here for a moment, in front of the blue door. This is the house where the poet lived for six years, and the room whose window you can see on the first floor is the one in which he wrote most of his early work. The man who owns the house today is a dentist, and he is used to visitors standing in the street and pointing. Now look to your left. The narrow lane that runs beside the house is older than the house itself. It is the only lane in this quarter which has never been widened, which is why it still floods every winter. At the end of it there is a café whose owner claims that his grandfather served coffee to the poet every morning. That may well be true. What is certainly true is that the chairs, which look old enough, were bought in two thousand and four. Walk to the end of the lane and wait there. The next stop is the school that gave this street its name.

b1-w11-bc0.speaker: Presenter
b1-w11-bc0.text: Welcome to the week in review. On Sunday the transport minister said that fuel prices would not rise before the summer. On Monday his office told a newspaper that he had been talking about diesel only. By Wednesday, petrol was up nine per cent. Layla, what happened?

b1-w11-bc1.speaker: Analyst
b1-w11-bc1.text: Two things happened. First, he said something narrower than people heard. He told the conference that there were no plans for an increase, and 'no plans' is not a promise. Second, nobody asked him the obvious follow-up question. If a journalist had asked him whether he meant petrol as well, we would have known on Sunday. Instead, three papers reported that he had promised prices would stay the same, and one reported that he had refused to comment, which was not true either. He did comment. He was simply careful.

b1-w11-bc3.speaker: Analyst
b1-w11-bc3.text: Everybody was a little wrong, which is the most uncomfortable answer there is.

b1-w12-bc0.speaker: Guide
b1-w12-bc0.text: Everything you are about to see is done in this one building. The glass arrives as sand, which surprises most visitors, and it is delivered by truck twice a week. The sand is mixed with two other materials, and then it is heated to about one thousand five hundred degrees. At that temperature it is not solid and it is not liquid; it is somewhere in between, and that is when it is shaped. The bottles you can see on the left were made about four minutes ago. They are still too hot to touch, so they are cooled slowly, over ninety minutes, in that long tunnel. If they were cooled quickly, they would crack. Every bottle is then checked by a camera that takes sixteen photographs of it. About one in forty is rejected, and the rejected ones are crushed and used again the same day. Nothing is thrown away. The factory was built in nineteen ninety-one, and it has been running seven days a week since two thousand and two.

b1-w13-bc0.speaker: Host
b1-w13-bc0.text: Our next caller has a problem that a lot of you wrote to us about. Go ahead, Kamal.

b1-w13-bc1.speaker: Kamal
b1-w13-bc1.text: I earn enough, I think, but there is never enough left at the end of the month. Both my sisters say I spend too much on small things, and neither of them is wrong. But I cannot see where it goes.

b1-w13-bc2.speaker: Host
b1-w13-bc2.text: That is the most common problem we get, and it is almost never the big things. Try this for one month. Write down every amount under fifty pounds, and only those. Most people track the rent and forget the rest, and the rest is usually too big to ignore. Second: you said you earn enough. Enough for what? If you have no number, any amount feels too little. Pick one goal, one figure and one date. Third, and this is the hard one: neither saving nor earning more will help if you do not know the shape of the month. Some weeks are far more expensive than others. Find the expensive week, and move something out of it.

b1-w13-bc3.speaker: Kamal
b1-w13-bc3.text: The expensive week is always the first one.

b1-w13-bc4.speaker: Host
b1-w13-bc4.text: Then you have just done the hardest part.

b1-w14-bc0.speaker: Teacher
b1-w14-bc0.text: This is the last morning, so I want to say one thing and then let you go. When you started, most of you wanted to learn English in order to get a better job. That is a good reason, and although it worked for some of you, it is not the reason you kept going. You kept going because you started enjoying being understood. That is a different thing, and it is much harder to lose. A warning, however. In three weeks you will stop practising. Not because you decide to, but because nothing will remind you. So decide now what will remind you. Some of you have agreed to meet on Fridays, and I would recommend keeping that, even when only two people come. Others plan to read for ten minutes a night, which sounds too small to matter and is in fact the only size that survives. Finally, avoid waiting to feel ready before you speak. Nobody feels ready. You did not feel ready in week one either, and yet here you are, understanding every word I am saying.

b2-w1-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w1-bc0.text: Good morning. Today I want to talk about why progress stops, and I want to be careful about a distinction that most people collapse. Consider two students. The first has studied English for six years. The second has been studying English for six years. In everyday speech we treat those as the same sentence. They are not. The first tells you about a completed quantity: six years exist, they are in the past, and something resulted. The second tells you about an unfinished activity, and it carries an implication the first does not, which is that the effort is still going on, and possibly going on longer than expected. Now, here is why this matters beyond grammar. We have known since the nineteen sixties that skill acquisition is not linear. What we have been discovering more recently is less comfortable: the plateau is not a failure of effort. Learners on a plateau have usually been working harder than they were at the start. They have been repeating what they already do well, because repeating what you do well feels like progress and feels safe. So the question to ask is not 'how long have you been studying?' It is 'what have you actually completed?' The first question measures your patience. The second measures your progress. Most of us have been answering the first one for years, and calling it the second.

b2-w2-bc0.speaker: Presenter
b2-w2-bc0.text: Tonight: the bridge that closed with four hours' notice, and the eighteen months of warnings that came before it. Our reporter has seen documents that nobody was supposed to see.

b2-w2-bc1.speaker: Reporter
b2-w2-bc1.text: By the time the bridge was closed on the fourth of March, engineers had been raising concerns for a year and a half. The first report, in September the year before, had described the western supports as 'deteriorating but stable'. That phrase matters, because it had allowed the authority to postpone a decision without technically ignoring the warning. A second inspection, in January, had removed the word 'stable'. Nobody, it seems, noticed that it had gone. What we have established is this. The engineers had not been silent. They had written, they had escalated, and by February two of them had asked to be removed from the project. The authority says it received no formal recommendation to close the bridge, and strictly speaking that is true. What it had received was three documents, each one more worried than the last, none of which used the word 'close'. One of them, dated the eleventh of February, ends with a sentence the authority has not explained to us. It reads: we consider our obligation discharged. Engineers do not write that about a bridge they believe is safe. The question, then, is not who failed to speak. It is why a system that had been told three times still needed a fourth.

b2-w2-bc2.speaker: Presenter
b2-w2-bc2.text: The authority declined to be interviewed. We will keep asking.

b2-w3-bc1.speaker: Tarek
b2-w3-bc1.text: Of course I kept it. Why would I throw it away?

b2-w3-bc2.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc2.text: Because you'd told me you had. That's why. In the car, on the way back from the hospital. You said you'd burnt everything.

b2-w3-bc3.speaker: Tarek
b2-w3-bc3.text: I said I'd burnt the letters.

b2-w3-bc5.speaker: Tarek
b2-w3-bc5.text: They were different. You know they were different. I'd been carrying those letters around for two years, and every time I read them I was worse afterwards. The photograph is just, it's the four of us on a beach. Nobody is angry in it.

b2-w3-bc6.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc6.text: That's exactly what's wrong with it. Sorry. That came out—

b2-w3-bc8.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc8.text: It's just that when I look at it, I don't see the four of us on a beach. I see the morning after. I see you standing in the kitchen not telling me. And I'd been asking you for a week. So when you keep it, and you put it in a drawer where I'd obviously find it—

b2-w3-bc9.speaker: Tarek
b2-w3-bc9.text: I didn't put it anywhere. It's been in that drawer since we moved. Mona. It's been in that drawer since we moved.

b2-w3-bc10.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc10.text: Do you remember what you actually said to me in that car?

b2-w3-bc12.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc12.text: That's not the same thing, and you know it isn't.

b2-w3-bc13.speaker: Tarek
b2-w3-bc13.text: No. It isn't. What I meant was, I'm not going to be the person who keeps a shrine. What I said was, I've burnt everything. Because the second one was shorter, and you were crying, and I wanted the conversation to be over.

b2-w3-bc14.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc14.text: It was over. For eight months it was completely over.

b2-w3-bc16.speaker: Mona
b2-w3-bc16.text: Fine. Then I'm the one who went looking.

b2-w4-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w4-bc0.text: Let me start with a number that will be wrong. By twenty-thirty, according to the projection on the screen, this city will have added two million people. I want to spend the next few minutes explaining why that figure will be wrong, and why it is still the most useful figure we have. First, what the projection actually says. It does not say two million people will arrive. It says that if the trends of the last twelve years continue, the city will have absorbed roughly that number by the end of the decade. By twenty-thirty we will have been building at the current rate for eighteen years. The projection is a sentence about our own behaviour, not about the future. Second, why it will be wrong. Every projection of this kind has been wrong, in both directions, and for the same reason: people respond to the projection. If the number frightens the planners, they will be building differently within three years, and the number will fall. If it reassures them, they will be doing nothing, and it will rise. A forecast that changes behaviour cannot describe the world it predicts. So why publish it? Because the alternative is not a better number. The alternative is planning with no number at all, which in practice means planning for the city that already exists. And by twenty-thirty, that city will have stopped existing.

b2-w5-bc0.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc0.text: If we'd said something in April, none of this would have happened.

b2-w5-bc1.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc1.text: That's not true, and you know it isn't. Because if we'd said something in April, they would have moved us both off the project and given it to Hana, and Hana would have signed exactly the same thing. It wouldn't have changed the outcome. It would have changed who was standing here.

b2-w5-bc2.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc2.text: So your position is that it wouldn't have mattered.

b2-w5-bc3.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc3.text: My position is that it wouldn't have worked. Those aren't the same thing.

b2-w5-bc5.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc5.text: Look. If I'd known in April what I know now, I'd have gone to the board directly. I would have. But in April all I had was a feeling that the numbers were too clean.

b2-w5-bc6.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc6.text: You told me they were too clean. In the car park. You said nobody's costs come in that tidy.

b2-w5-bc8.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc8.text: And I said we should check. And you said, let's see what the second quarter looks like.

b2-w5-bc9.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc9.text: Which was a reasonable thing to say in April.

b2-w5-bc10.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc10.text: It was a reasonable thing to say if you wanted to not know for another three months. That's what it was for. If either of us had genuinely thought the numbers were fine, we wouldn't have needed to wait for the second quarter to find out.

b2-w5-bc11.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc11.text: That's a hard way to put it.

b2-w5-bc12.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc12.text: It's the accurate way to put it. So don't tell me it wouldn't have worked. Tell me we didn't try.

b2-w5-bc13.speaker: Sami
b2-w5-bc13.text: All right. We didn't try. That doesn't make it better.

b2-w5-bc14.speaker: Layla
b2-w5-bc14.text: No. But it makes it ours.

b2-w6-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w6-bc0.text: Historians are trained to distrust a certain kind of sentence, and I want to defend it anyway. The sentence is: if that had not happened, we would not be here. Notice the shape of it. The condition is in the past; the consequence is in the present. If the treaty had been signed in eighteen seventy, this region would be a single country today. If she had not missed that train, you would not exist. These are mixed conditionals, and they are the natural grammar of historical explanation, which is why historians use them constantly while officially disapproving of them. The objection is reasonable. We cannot test them. If the treaty had been signed, a thousand other things would also have changed, and we cannot hold those still while we vary the one we are interested in. So the sentence looks like an argument and behaves like a story. But consider the alternative. If we refuse all counterfactuals, we lose the ability to say that anything mattered. To say that a decision was important is to say that the present would be different without it. There is no other content to the word 'important'. A history with no counterfactuals is not a more rigorous history; it is a chronicle, a list of things that happened in order, and it cannot distinguish the treaty from the weather that afternoon. So: use them, and say out loud that you are using them. The danger is not the sentence. The danger is the sentence pretending to be a fact.

b2-w7-bc2.speaker: Hana
b2-w7-bc2.text: March. Since March, and you told Amir.

b2-w7-bc3.speaker: Father
b2-w7-bc3.text: I wish you wouldn't look at me like that. I didn't tell Amir. Amir works at the hospital. Amir found out, which is not the same thing.

b2-w7-bc4.speaker: Hana
b2-w7-bc4.text: If only you'd said something. One sentence. Hana, I've had some tests.

b2-w7-bc5.speaker: Father
b2-w7-bc5.text: And then what? You'd have come back from Dubai, you'd have lost the contract, and you'd have sat in this flat for six months watching me have tests. I wish I could tell you I'd have handled it better than you would have. I wouldn't.

b2-w7-bc6.speaker: Hana
b2-w7-bc6.text: That was my decision to make.

b2-w7-bc7.speaker: Father
b2-w7-bc7.text: Yes. It was. That's the part I got wrong. I keep wishing I'd been the sort of father you could have told bad news to. Then maybe I'd have been the sort you could hear it from.

b2-w7-bc9.speaker: Father
b2-w7-bc9.text: Don't. Not yet. Ask me the medical question. You've been holding it since you walked in.

b2-w7-bc10.speaker: Hana
b2-w7-bc10.text: What did they say on Thursday?

b2-w7-bc11.speaker: Father
b2-w7-bc11.text: They said it's operable. They said Tuesday. I wish it were sooner. And before you say it: yes, I have already told your mother, and no, I did not tell her first. She asked me the same question you did, in the same voice, standing in the same place. You are more like her than either of you would like.

b2-w8-bc0.speaker: Host
b2-w8-bc0.text: Last night's interview has been described as a collapse, a trap and, by one newspaper this morning, as the most honest four minutes in a decade. Rania, you were in the room. What was she actually asked?

b2-w8-bc1.speaker: Rania
b2-w8-bc1.text: She was asked three things, and the order matters. She was first asked whether the department had approved the payments. She said it had not. She was then asked whether she personally had seen the file. She said she couldn't recall. And she was finally asked, and this is the question everyone has forgotten, whether she would resign if it turned out that she had. She said she would.

b2-w8-bc2.speaker: Host
b2-w8-bc2.text: Karim, why has that third question disappeared from the coverage?

b2-w8-bc3.speaker: Karim
b2-w8-bc3.text: Because it doesn't fit either story. Those who want her gone are reporting that she denied everything, which she didn't; she made a commitment. Those defending her are reporting that she was ambushed, which she wasn't; she was asked a hypothetical and she chose to answer it. She could have said 'I won't deal in hypotheticals'. Ministers say that eleven times a day. She didn't.

b2-w8-bc4.speaker: Rania
b2-w8-bc4.text: I would add one thing. The word 'approved' was doing a lot of work in that first answer. She was asked whether the department had approved the payments, and she said it had not. Nobody asked her whether the payments had been made. Those are different questions, and she answered the one she was given, precisely and, as far as I can tell, truthfully.

b2-w8-bc5.speaker: Karim
b2-w8-bc5.text: Which is what makes the interview interesting rather than damaging. She was not caught out. She was unusually careful, and then, in the last thirty seconds, she was not.

b2-w8-bc6.speaker: Rania
b2-w8-bc6.text: She also asked the interviewer a question, which nobody has reported. She asked him whether he had the file.

b2-w9-bc0.speaker: Anchor
b2-w9-bc0.text: Good evening. Water pressure has been restored to most of the eastern districts tonight, twelve hours after a main was ruptured during construction work. Around forty thousand homes were affected. The company says the pipe had been marked on the plans, and that the contractor has been suspended while the incident is investigated. Our correspondent is in Zeitoun.

b2-w9-bc1.speaker: Correspondent
b2-w9-bc1.text: The pipe was cut at about six this morning. Within an hour the street had been closed, and by nine the water had been shut off across four districts. What has angered people here is not the accident, because accidents happen. It is that they were not told. The company's message was sent to registered mobile numbers only, and in this district most accounts were opened before that system existed. So thousands of people had their supply cut with no warning at all. Several residents told me they had their tanks filled by neighbours who happened to have heard.

b2-w9-bc3.speaker: Correspondent
b2-w9-bc3.text: The section is being replaced tonight rather than patched, which is why it has taken longer. It should be finished by morning. Schools in the four districts have been told to open as normal, and the two hospitals were never affected; they have their own tanks. The wider question, how many other pipes are marked on plans that contractors are not required to check, has not been answered, and it was not asked at this afternoon's press conference either.

b2-w10-bc0.speaker: Narrator
b2-w10-bc0.text: For eleven years the case was closed. It was reopened in twenty-nineteen, not because new evidence appeared, but because someone re-read the old evidence and noticed what it could not mean. Here is the reasoning, and I want you to follow it rather than accept it. The gate was locked from the inside. So whoever left must have had a key, or must have climbed the eastern wall. The wall was wet that night and unmarked in the morning, so they cannot have climbed it. Therefore they must have had a key. Eleven people had keys. But the original investigation had reached a different conclusion. It decided the gate might have been locked afterwards, by a caretaker who could simply have forgotten doing it. That is not impossible. Caretakers do forget. And once you allow that, the key stops mattering and the eleven names dissolve. This is the part that should trouble you. Both lines of reasoning are valid. One assumes the physical evidence is reliable and human memory is not; the other assumes the opposite. Neither can be tested now. What decided the case in nineteen ninety-eight was not evidence. It was which of those two assumptions the investigating officer found more natural, and he had been a caretaker himself, twenty years earlier, in a building with a gate he had sometimes forgotten to lock. He may never have noticed that about his own reasoning. Most of us don't.

b2-w11-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w11-bc0.text: The building we are looking at, begun in nineteen thirty-two and never completed, is the most instructive failure in the city. Its architect, who had never built anything above three storeys, won the competition with a drawing rather than a plan, a distinction which the committee, most of whom were merchants, did not recognise as important. The design, admired even now for its staircase, contains a mistake visible only in section. The light wells, intended to serve the inner rooms, narrow as they descend. Anyone standing on the ground floor, looking up, sees a bright rectangle of sky. Anyone in the rooms beside them sees almost nothing. The architect, drawing in elevation, never drew the section that would have shown him this. Two things follow, neither of them about architecture. First, the failure was not one of talent; the staircase is genuinely beautiful. It was a failure of representation. He was working in a medium which could not display the error he was making. Second, the committee's mistake was the more serious one, and it is the one we repeat. They judged the thing they were shown, rather than asking what they were not being shown. Every profession has a section drawing it does not habitually make. Finding yours, which is difficult and unrewarding, is most of what expertise consists of.

b2-w12-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w12-bc0.text: There is a small group of English verbs which change meaning depending on what follows them, and I want to use them to make a point about memory rather than about grammar. Compare: I remembered to lock the door, and I remembered locking the door. The first is about an intention that was carried out. The second is about a past event being recalled. Native speakers use them correctly without being able to explain the difference, which is normal, and learners often produce the second when they mean the first, which is not a small error. It is the difference between a plan and a memory. Now the interesting part. Psychologists studying false memory have found that the second construction is unusually dangerous. When people are asked do you remember locking the door, they reconstruct the event, and reconstruction feels identical to recall. When they are asked did you intend to lock the door, they do not reconstruct anything; they consult a plan, and plans are easier to check. So the grammatical distinction that learners find fiddly turns out to mark a real difference in how reliable the answer is. I am not going to tell you that this makes the grammar easier. It does not. But it explains why the distinction survived. Languages tend to keep the contrasts that do work, and the contrast between having intended something and having witnessed it does a great deal of work.

b2-w13-bc0.speaker: Host
b2-w13-bc0.text: Every guest on this programme this month has told me what most people want. Dalia, you actually measure it.

b2-w13-bc1.speaker: Dalia
b2-w13-bc1.text: And that is why I almost never use the phrase. 'Most people' is doing something dishonest in nearly every sentence it appears in. Take last week's figure: sixty-one per cent support the scheme. That is most people, in a sense. But of those sixty-one, fewer than half could describe what the scheme does, and a third said they would oppose it if it raised their own costs, which it will. So 'most people support it' is both true and useless.

b2-w13-bc2.speaker: Minister
b2-w13-bc2.text: With respect, all of politics works like that. Neither of us has a better instrument. Every mandate in every parliament rests on a number that thin.

b2-w13-bc3.speaker: Dalia
b2-w13-bc3.text: I agree, and that is not a defence. It is the problem. The honest sentence is longer: a majority express support, few understand the detail, and support falls sharply when costs are mentioned. Nobody puts that on a poster.

b2-w13-bc4.speaker: Minister
b2-w13-bc4.text: Because a poster with that on it loses.

b2-w13-bc5.speaker: Host
b2-w13-bc5.text: So is there any question where the answer is stable?

b2-w13-bc6.speaker: Dalia
b2-w13-bc6.text: Yes. Almost all of them, if you ask twice, six months apart, and count only the people who say the same thing both times. That group is usually about a quarter. Every serious campaign is fought over the other three quarters, and each of them will tell you that they are most people.

b2-w14-bc0.speaker: Lecturer
b2-w14-bc0.text: I want to make an argument in four moves, and I want to signal each move as I make it, because the signalling is the lesson. First, the claim. Discourse markers are not decoration. 'However' is not a more formal 'but'. It performs a different act: it tells the listener that what follows will not merely differ from what preceded, but will outweigh it. Second, the evidence. When we removed the markers from recorded lectures and played them to students, comprehension of the individual sentences was unaffected. Recall of the argument's direction fell by roughly forty per cent. The students could tell you what had been said. They could not tell you which side the speaker was on. Third, and this is the concession, which I am flagging deliberately, the effect is smaller in writing. Readers can go back. Listeners cannot. So it is possible to write reasonably well while using markers carelessly, which is why many fluent writers are poor lecturers. Nevertheless, and here is the fourth move, the conclusion is stronger than the concession. If your listener cannot reconstruct the shape of your argument, you have not made an argument; you have produced a sequence of true sentences. And notice what I did just then. I said 'nevertheless', and you knew, before you heard any of the content, that the concession was about to be overruled. That is the whole mechanism, and it cost me one word.

b2-w15-bc0.speaker: Samira
b2-w15-bc0.text: It wasn't the audit that worried me. It was how calm you were about the audit.

b2-w15-bc1.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc1.text: I'm calm about a lot of things.

b2-w15-bc2.speaker: Samira
b2-w15-bc2.text: Not about this. What you do when something's wrong is you tidy. You alphabetise. For three weeks you didn't tidy anything.

b2-w15-bc4.speaker: Samira
b2-w15-bc4.text: No. Karim. It was you who called them.

b2-w15-bc5.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc5.text: It was me who called them.

b2-w15-bc7.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc7.text: What I couldn't do was watch it happen twice. That's all it was. It wasn't loyalty to the company and it certainly wasn't courage. I did it in a car park at eleven at night and I was sick afterwards.

b2-w15-bc9.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc9.text: Because what you'd have done is come with me. And then it would have been the two of us in that car park, and one of us needed to still be here in six months.

b2-w15-bc11.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc11.text: No. It's the second time this year someone has told me that.

b2-w15-bc12.speaker: Nour
b2-w15-bc12.text: It was Hana, wasn't it. The first time.

b2-w15-bc14.speaker: Nour
b2-w15-bc14.text: Does she know you did it?

b2-w15-bc15.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc15.text: What Hana knows is that somebody did it, and that whoever it was waited eight months longer than she did. She hasn't asked me. I think that's deliberate.

b2-w15-bc16.speaker: Samira
b2-w15-bc16.text: It was her they moved to the Alexandria office, wasn't it.

b2-w15-bc17.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc17.text: It was. And what I keep coming back to is that nobody moved me anywhere. Which tells you something about how much they think I matter, and it isn't flattering.

b2-w15-bc18.speaker: Samira
b2-w15-bc18.text: Right. So what happens on Monday?

b2-w15-bc19.speaker: Karim
b2-w15-bc19.text: On Monday, nothing happens. It's what happens in March that I can't tell you about.

b2-w16-bc0.speaker: Interviewer
b2-w16-bc0.text: Ms Farid, thank you for making time. Could you outline for us the rationale behind the decision to withdraw the product?

b2-w16-bc1.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc1.text: Certainly. Following a routine review, we concluded that the product no longer aligned with our long-term strategic priorities, and we took the decision to discontinue it in an orderly manner.

b2-w16-bc2.speaker: Interviewer
b2-w16-bc2.text: And the reports of a safety concern?

b2-w16-bc3.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc3.text: I'm not in a position to comment on speculation.

b2-w16-bc4.speaker: Interviewer
b2-w16-bc4.text: Thank you. Right, that's us. We're done. Ahmed, you can put that down.

b2-w16-bc7.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc7.text: Right, look. Between us, it fell apart. Not the product, the whole thing. We'd been putting off the review for a year and a half because nobody wanted to be the one who brought it up, and then someone finally did, and it turned out we'd all been quietly assuming somebody else had checked. Nobody had.

b2-w16-bc9.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc9.text: It's a much worse answer, which is exactly why you got the other one. I'm not going to be the person who says 'nobody had checked' on camera.

b2-w16-bc10.speaker: Interviewer
b2-w16-bc10.text: You realise the strategic-priorities line is what everyone will run.

b2-w16-bc11.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc11.text: Of course they'll run it. It's clean, it's short, and it doesn't require anybody to ring me back. And in eighteen months, when somebody digs it up and puts it next to whatever comes out of the review, I'll be the one explaining why I said it. I know exactly what I've just bought and what it cost.

b2-w16-bc12.speaker: Interviewer
b2-w16-bc12.text: Off the record, then. Will you pull the next one earlier?

b2-w16-bc13.speaker: Ms Farid
b2-w16-bc13.text: We'll see. Ask me again in a year and I'll give you a sentence you can use.

a1-w1-bc0.speaker: Omar
a1-w1-bc0.text: Hello. My name is Omar. I am from Cairo, in Egypt. I am twenty-five years old. I am a student. This is my friend. His name is Ali. He is from Alexandria. He is not a student. He is a teacher. We are in the same English class. Our class is on Monday and Wednesday. It is at six o'clock. Ali is a very good friend. Nice to meet you. Goodbye!

a1-w2-bc0.speaker: Salma
a1-w2-bc0.text: This is my family. I have got two sisters and one brother. My brother's name is Karim. He is ten years old. My sisters are Hana and Nour. Hana is my big sister. She has got a small car. Nour is my little sister. She has got a cat. Its name is Mimi. My mother is a nurse. My father works in a shop. Our house is small, but it is very happy.

a1-w3-bc0.speaker: Teacher
a1-w3-bc0.text: Good morning. Here is your day. There are three classes today. The first class is at nine o'clock. There is a break at eleven. The second class is at half past eleven. Lunch is at one o'clock. The last class is at three. There are twenty students in the class today. Tomorrow is Friday, and there are no classes on Friday. Have a good day!

a1-w4-bc0.speaker: A man in the street
a1-w4-bc0.text: Excuse me? Yes. Listen. Go out of this building. Turn left. Walk to the end of the street. The pharmacy is next to the bank. It is opposite the big mosque. It is not far. Five minutes. There is a bus stop in front of it. If you see the school, you are too far. Go back. The pharmacy is open now. Thank you!

a1-w5-bc0.speaker: Sami
a1-w5-bc0.text: I get up at six o'clock every day. I drink tea and I eat bread with cheese. I go to work at seven. I work in an office with my friends. We start at eight. We have lunch at one. I finish work at four. I come home and I sleep for one hour. In the evening I study English. I go to bed at eleven. On Friday I do not work. I visit my family.

a1-w6-bc0.speaker: Youssef
a1-w6-bc0.text: My sister Hana likes food very much. She eats rice and chicken every day. She does not eat fish. She drinks coffee in the morning and tea in the evening. a1-w7-bc0.speaker: Market announcer
a1-w7-bc0.text: Welcome to the market. Listen to today's prices. Bread is three pounds. How much is the rice? The rice is twelve pounds for one kilo. The tomatoes are eight pounds. Come early!

a1-w8-bc0.speaker: Mona
a1-w8-bc0.text: My friend Nadia is tall and she has got long black hair. She is twenty years old. She is very kind and she is always happy. She has got a big blue bag. Her bag is old, but she loves it. Nadia has got a new phone. It is small and white. She lives in a big flat with her family. Her flat is near my house. Nadia is a good friend.

a1-w9-bc0.speaker: Ahmed
a1-w9-bc0.text: Hello, I am Ahmed. I can swim and I can drive a car. I can't cook. My food is not good! I like playing football with my friends on Friday. I love watching films at home. I don't like running. My brother can play the guitar, but I can't. He likes singing. I want to learn. Can you play music? Tell me!

a1-w10-bc0.speaker: Nour
a1-w10-bc0.text: Yesterday was my birthday. I was very happy. My family was at home with me. My mother was in the kitchen all morning. There was a big cake on the table. It was chocolate. My friends were here at six o'clock. We were together for three hours. There were ten people in my small flat! My little brother was very excited. It was a good day. Today I am tired, but I am happy.
